SpaceX is setting the stage for Flight 8 — and beyond
SpaceX's Starship rocket prototypes are seen at the SpaceX Starbase in Brownsville, Texas, in August 2023.
Veronica G. Cardenas/Reuters
During the broadcast of SpaceX’s November test launch, Flight 6, SpaceX engineers Jessie Anderson and Kate Tice said the company was finishing construction of a 1 million-square-foot “Starfactory” in South Texas. The goal for that structure is to allow the company to manufacture “hundreds of ships per year,” Anderson said.
SpaceX envisions it will need a large fleet of Super Heavy boosters — and an even larger stable of Starship spacecraft.
That’s because the Starship vehicles “will be staying in space for long duration missions to go to the moon or Mars or become tankers for refueling,” Anderson said. “But the boosters will come back and turn around to launch the next ship.”
“That (production cadence) might sound crazy,” Tice noted. “And that’s because it is.”
SpaceX is already known to keep a “garden” of rockets at its facilities in South Texas. At any given time, the area can be seen strewn with Starships and Super Heavy boosters.
On Thursday, SpaceX confirmed it already has a stable of hardware ready for yet another flight test: “The ship and booster for Starship’s eighth flight test are built and going through prelaunch testing and preparing to fly as we continue a rapid iterative development process to build a fully and rapidly reusable space transportation system,” the company said in a statement.

What could Musk's new role mean for the space regulatory environment?
Elon Musk attends a meeting at the Hyatt Regency on Capitol Hill in Washington, DC, on November 13, 2024.
Andrew Harnik/Getty Images
For years, there has appeared to be no love lost between SpaceX CEO Elon Musk and the Federal Aviation Administration, which licenses commercial rocket launches.
Musk has repeatedly used X, the social media platform formerly known as Twitter that he purchased two years ago for $44 billion, to blast the FAA and accuse the agency of holding up Starship testing.
In a September 17
post
, he threatened to sue the agency for “regulatory overreach.”
Musk has also alleged that the agency’s activities have been “
politically motivated
” to punish SpaceX.
Notably, Musk was also tapped by President-elect Donald Trump to run a new “Department of Government Efficiency.” Musk’s
goals
are to downsize the federal budget and operations by slashing spending,
curbing regulations
and
cutting the workforce
.
And it’s not yet clear how those goals might impact the FAA — or the agency’s role in the commercial space industry.
Launching a rocket requires companies to get the agency’s blessing, and the FAA also oversees investigations into rocket mishaps, such as the one that occurred with SpaceX’s Starship on Thursday.
Trump’s inauguration takes place Monday. Musk is expected to be in attendance.

How SpaceX's and Blue Origin's weeks are shaping up
Today has been a
wild
ride for the space industry.
Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin debuted its massive New Glenn rocket this morning. It safely reached orbit but failed to land its booster.
SpaceX’s problems were somewhat the opposite: There was a safe booster landing, but the company’s Starship spacecraft fell far short of its goal.
But New Glenn and Starship don’t quite offer an apples-to-apples comparison.
Blue Origin spent more than a decade tediously hashing out New Glenn’s design, aiming to all but ensure it would fly safely on the first mission.
SpaceX, meanwhile, has long been candid about how it embraces fiery mishaps during rocket development. And these Starship flights have always been billed as part of a testing and development effort — so perfection need not apply.
Zooming out, Starship is also a much more powerful launch vehicle than New Glenn. Musk has said he hopes Starship will be able to haul convoys of people to the moon and Mars.
While still a hefty vehicle, New Glenn is better aligned to compete with SpaceX’s Falcon rockets, which have been flying routine missions for years.
If you’re looking to keep score, however, it’s also important to note that recovering rocket boosters after takeoff if just a bonus when it comes to spaceflight. SpaceX is currently the only company in the world that does it routinely — and Blue Origin is attempting to replicate that success.
Still, to deem a mission successful, a rocket needs to take care of the real business: Safely delivering cargo to space. And while Starship was only carrying dummy payloads meant to simulate how it might deploy a satellite, the company didn’t get to test out that technology.
So by the big metrics, Bezos had a very good week.
Link Copied!
Starship still has a long road ahead
While SpaceX has made considerable progress — drastically improving Starship’s performance across test flights carried out since April 2023 — there’s still a lot to get done.
Each test flight improvement sets the company up to begin tackling more ambitious projects. And the company has some lofty line items on its to-do list this year.
“In 2025, SpaceX plans to undertake a long-duration flight test and a propellant transfer flight test,” according to a recent
report
from NASA’s Office of the Inspector General, or OIG.
Demonstrating the ability to launch a Starship into orbit and then rendezvous the spacecraft with a tanker carrying fuel is considered essential to the success of NASA’s Artemis program.
For NASA’s Artemis III mission — which aims to return astronauts to the moon for the first time since the Apollo era — Starship may need to dock with more than a dozen fuel tankers before continuing its mission to the lunar surface.
SpaceX will also face a “critical design review” for the Artemis III mission next summer, according to the OIG. Artemis III has already been subject to delays. Most recently, NASA said it will take off no earlier than
mid-2027
.
Musk also said in 2020 that he hopes SpaceX will launch “hundreds of missions” with satellites before attempting a crewed Starship mission.
As indicated by SpaceX attempting to fly Starlink simulators on this test flight, the company intends to use Starship to deploy batches of its internet-beaming satellites.
Also on the to-do list is figuring out how to land and re-fly the upper Starship spacecraft. The company has made headway hashing out the recovery of the Super Heavy booster. But so far, Starship has been left to sink to a watery grave in the ocean after each mission.
Link Copied!
Astrophysicist: Starship blew up over the Bahamas
Jonathan McDowell, an astrophysicist and astronomer at the Harvard-Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics, just ran some numbers attempting to confirm where — exactly — SpaceX’s Starship spacecraft might have blown up.
The “rapid unscheduled disassembly” — as SpaceX calls it — “happened over Bahamas, debris passing over Turks and Caicos a couple minutes later at ~120 km altitude (~75 miles),” according to his trajectory analysis, McDowell wrote in a message to CNN.
“Debris probably fell a few min after than in the sea north of Puerto Rico and the British Virgin Islands,” he writes.
Link Copied!
Found Starship debris? Call SpaceX
SpaceX is reminding members of the public to contact the company directly if you believe you have found a piece of hardware from a Starship launch.
If you believe you have identified a piece of debris, please
do not attempt to handle or retrieve the debris directly
. Instead, please contact your local authorities or the SpaceX Debris Hotline at 1-866-623-0234 or at recovery@spacex.com.

SpaceX and the FAA will investigate the mishap
SpaceX plans to work alongside federal regulators to conduct a “thorough investigation” into what went wrong with the Starship spacecraft during today’s test flight, the company said in a statement. The Federal Aviation Administration, which licenses commercial rocket launches and typically oversees such investigations, did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the matter.
Such an investigation could lengthen the time between test flights as officials hash out what went wrong and issue corrective actions SpaceX must take.
FAA-related delays with Starship have frequently drawn Musk’s ire. However, on Thursday, Musk said in one social media
post
that, based on a “preliminary” look at the problem, “Nothing so far suggests pushing next launch past next month.”
SpaceX has been angling to rapidly increase how often Starship flies.
Already, the company has hardware prepared for an eighth test flight, according to SpaceX’s statement.
That hardware is “built and going through prelaunch testing and preparing to fly as we continue a rapid iterative development process to build a fully and rapidly reusable space transportation system,” the statement reads.
The company also shared an oft-repeated refrain about how it wants the public to view mishaps during Starship test flights. They are learning experiences, the company emphasized.
“As always, success comes from what we learn, and this flight test will help us improve Starship’s reliability as SpaceX seeks to make life multiplanetary. Data review is already underway as we seek out root cause. We will conduct a thorough investigation, in coordination with the FAA, and implement corrective actions to make improvements on future Starship flight tests.”
Link Copied!
SpaceX: A fire broke out at the rear of the ship, causing the explosion
SpaceX just published a detailed recap of the successes and losses of today’s test flight.
In a 420-word post on its
website
, the company acknowledged that this mission was designed to put “a redesigned and upgraded Starship through a rigorous set of flight demonstrations.”
“It served as a reminder that development testing by definition is unpredictable,” the statement reads.
The company confirmed that it lost contact with the Starship spacecraft about eight and a half minutes into flight, and a “fire developed in the aft section of the ship” — causing the vehicle to explode, or a “rapid unscheduled disassembly” in SpaceX parlance.
The debris fell “into the Atlantic Ocean within the predefined hazard areas,” the company said.
The Federal Aviation Administration, however, acknowledged in an email to CNN that it activated a “Debris Response Area” after Starship exploded. Such a step is only taken if debris falls outside of areas that were closed to air traffic, according to the agency.

See how Starship stacks up to other rockets
You may have heard Starship is the biggest rocket ever created. And it is — by a long shot.
Starship stands at nearly 400 feet (121 meters) tall and packs 16.7 million pounds (7,590 tons) of force at liftoff.
Let’s compare that to some others among the largest rockets ever constructed — past and present.
Ian Berry/CNN
Falcon Heavy
: SpaceX’s own 230-foot-tall (70-meter-tall)
rocket
that previously held the title for
most powerful operational rocket
in the world. It has about 5 million pounds of thrust or roughly one-third of Starship’s power.
Saturn V
: The famous NASA rocket that powered the Apollo moon landings of the 20th century put out about
7.6 million pounds of thrust
at takeoff. That’s still less than half of Starship’s expected power, and the company has said upgrades could give Starship three times the thrust of the Saturn V. It stood at about 360 feet (110 meters) tall.
The Space Shuttle
: NASA’s workhorse launch system in the post-Apollo era, the shuttle had two solid rocket boosters that gave off about 5.3 million pounds of force at liftoff. It was about 180 feet (55 meters) tall.
Space Launch System
: NASA’s new moon rocket, which made its debut launch in 2022, is currently the
most powerful rocket in operation
. It produces about
8.8 million pounds of thrust
— just over half the Starship’s expected output. It’s 212 feet (65 meters) tall.
Russian N1 rocket
: This was Russia’s megamoon rocket of the 20th-century space race. And while it was never operational (all four launch attempts failed), Musk has said it’s the closest relative of Starship’s design. The N1 was expected to give off more than
10 million pounds of thrust
at liftoff — still 40% less than Starship.
New Glenn
: The brand new rocket developed by Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin can pack up to
3.8 million pounds
of thrust during take off. That’s significantly less than the others on this list, in part because New Glenn is designed to be a “heavy lift” rocket, which isn’t quite the same category as Starship, which has been dubbed “super heavy lift.” New Glenn made its
launch debut in the early hours of Thursday morning
.
Link Copied!
Starship is key to SpaceX's long-term ambitions
A NASA artist’s illustration of Artemis astronauts working on the moon.
NASA
SpaceX — and NASA — have huge goals for this rocket.
NASA wants to use Starship to carry out the final leg of the journey to put astronauts back on the moon for the first time in five decades as part of its Artemis program. The space agency gave SpaceX a
$2.9 billion contract
in 2021 to get the job done, and it inked another $1 billion
deal
after that.
The first crewed moon landing for Starship could take place as soon as mid-2027, according to NASA’s latest
timeline
.
Starship is also the linchpin of SpaceX’s goal of getting humans to Mars. The company’s founding purpose is to make humans a multi-planetary species, sending them to live on other planets in case Earth becomes unsuitable for life.
That task would require a truly massive rocket.
“We are trying to build something that is capable of creating a permanent base on the moon and a city on Mars — that’s why it is so large,” SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said in 2023.
Whether that goal is feasible —
economically, technologically and politically
— remains to be seen. But Musk and SpaceX have garnered a diehard fanbase rallied around the idea.
Here are some other items on the agenda for Starship:
Send paying customers (or space tourists) on trips to deep space: At least one customer —
billionaire Jared Isaacman
, who was recently picked to serve as NASA chief under President-elect Donald Trump, is spearheading a development program alongside SpaceX and plans to one day fly aboard Starship.
Launch batches of SpaceX’s
Starlink
satellites, which beam internet service across the globe
Potentially launch new scientific instruments, such as space-based telescopes

Elon Musk: A propellant leak was the likely culprit
SpaceX chief Elon Musk just shared “preliminary” analysis about what might have caused the Starship spacecraft to fail roughly 10 minutes into flight.
Preliminary indication is that we had an oxygen/fuel leak in the cavity above the ship engine firewall that was large enough to build pressure in excess of the vent capacity.
Apart from obviously double-checking for leaks, we will add fire suppression to that volume and…
— Elon Musk (@elonmusk)
January 17, 2025
Liquid oxygen is used as an oxidizer on Starship, allowing the engines to breathe fire as the fuel, liquid methane, is burned. Both liquid oxygen and methane make up the propellants used by Starship’s Raptor rocket engines.

Federal regulators "slowed and diverted" aircraft
In a statement, the Federal Aviation Adminsitration acknowledged that it “briefly slowed and diverted aircraft around the area where space vehicle debris was falling.”
“Normal operations have resumed,” the statement, shared with CNN at 7:48 p.m. ET, reads.
The FAA activates a “Debris Response Area” when rockets or spacecraft disintegrate or explode outside a predetermined safety zone.
During rocket launches, regulators routinely issue warnings to air and maritime traffic — warning boaters and pilots to stay away from the launch site. But Starship broke apart fairly late in its flight path — about 10 minutes after takeoff.
It had already climbed 90 miles (146 kilometers) in altitude and was traveling at 13,200 miles per hour (21,317 kilometers per hour), according to the last telemetry data shared by SpaceX.

This is what we know so far about Starship's destruction
Orange balls of light fly across the sky, leaving a trail of smoke behind as debris from a SpaceX rocket launched in Texas is spotted over Port-Au-Prince, Haiti, on Thursday.
Reuters TV
SpaceX has had a solid track record on the past few test flights of guiding Starship to a controlled landing at its target destination in the Indian Ocean.
Today’s failure was somewhat unexpected — but SpaceX did say it was testing substantial upgrades on this vehicle: It was larger in size due to SpaceX installing larger fuel tanks, for example, and had a new flight computer and upgraded avionics.
Just to recap: The Starship spacecraft, often referred to simply as the “ship,” seemed to go smoothly for the first several minutes. About two and a half minutes into flight, the vehicle safely separated from the Super Heavy booster and lit up its own six engines.
After flying on its own for about five minutes, one of the three inner engines — arranged in a circle inside three other engines optimized for the vacuum of space — flamed out.
Seconds later, more engines began to flame out, according to graphics shown on the SpaceX livestream.
By the 8 minutes, 30 second mark — five of the six engines were offline and the tone of SpaceX’s broadcast began to change, shifting from roaring cheers to concerned dispatches about the “ship status.”
About 10 minutes later, the webcast hosts, SpaceX’s Dan Huot and Kate Tice, confirmed that Starship was lost.

Here's how Starship debris is affecting air traffic
From CNN's Pete Muntean
The disintegration of SpaceX’s Starship rocket is certainly delaying commercial flights in Florida.
The Federal Aviation Administration says flights departing Miami International Airport and Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International Airport are being delayed an average of an hour due to a “rocket launch anomaly.”
A separate FAA alert says flights are delayed due to “debris.”
The flight tracking site Flightradar24 shows several planes rerouting or holding near the area where Starship was destroyed.
